intro: Twenty findings from the budget vs outcomes data, ranked by how much they should change what a careful reader believes. Each was re-run under alternative deflators, year ranges and definitions; the verdict says whether it held. Unusual is not improper: these are patterns worth discussing, not conclusions about conduct.

insights.title: Fire/EMS calls rose 51% while real Fire spending rose 16%
insights.dek: Dispatched calls grew from 121,148 in FY2013 to 182,458 in FY2025. Fire's spending, after inflation, grew a third as fast, and the median response to a life-threatening medical call is about a minute slower.
insights.why_it_matters: Response time is the outcome residents feel most directly. When demand grows three times faster than resources, the choice is between more units, different dispatch rules or accepting slower arrivals; the budget documents do not make that choice explicit.
insights.surprise: Fire is usually described as a department whose budget grows relentlessly. In real terms it grew slower than the General Fund as a whole (+40% per resident).

insights.title: General Fund spending per resident rose 40% after inflation, then went flat
insights.dek: Real General Fund operating spending per resident went from $5,472 in FY2013 to $7,656 in FY2025. Nearly all of the growth happened by FY2021; the last four years are within 3% of each other.
insights.why_it_matters: Per-resident, inflation-adjusted spending is the fairest single measure of how much more government the city buys. A plateau since FY2021 is a different story from the 'runaway budget' story and the 'austerity' story both told in public debate.
insights.surprise: Nominal spending kept rising after FY2021; the flat line only appears after inflation, which ran 4–6% a year in FY2022–23.

insights.title: Targets were eased after 21% of misses, but after only 5% of hits
insights.dek: Across 5,199 year-over-year target changes, departments lowered the bar four times as often after missing it. Raising a target was the more common response to a hit.
insights.why_it_matters: A performance target only means something if it is not adjusted to fit the result. The pattern is consistent with departments treating targets as forecasts rather than commitments, which is a legitimate practice, but it should be stated.
insights.surprise: The effect is not concentrated in a few departments: 34 of 35 departments with enough changes show it.

insights.title: Police overtime has run at more than twice its adopted budget every year since FY2019
insights.dek: FY2025 payroll overtime reached $147M against an adopted budget of $64M, 2.3 times. The gap widened after FY2022 as sworn headcount fell below its authorized level.
insights.why_it_matters: Overtime is how the city buys police hours it did not budget for. A gap this persistent means the adopted budget is not the operative plan; the real decision happens in mid-year supplementals that get less scrutiny.
insights.surprise: Per hour, overtime is not obviously more expensive than hiring: the fully loaded cost ratio is between 0.83 and 1.07 depending on benefit assumptions.

insights.title: HSH spending is 2.8 times its FY2017 level after inflation; no other big department doubled
insights.dek: HSH's real spending went from $380M in its first full year to $1.06B in FY2025. The next fastest large department, Public Health, grew 40%.
insights.why_it_matters: A department that nearly triples in eight years is a policy choice made in the open, but its measures are new and its baselines short. Whether outcomes moved in step is the question the scorecard should answer and mostly cannot yet.

insights.title: Seven years after voters approved it, the Seawall bond had spent 13% of its money
insights.dek: Of the $425M Embarcadero Seawall bond approved in 2018, $56M was spent by June 2025 (14% with commitments). Bonds of similar age had spent 33% to 93%.
insights.why_it_matters: Voters approve bonds against a stated program and pace. Slow spending can be prudent sequencing or a stalled project; either way, the interest and the risk keep accruing and the pace is rarely reported back to voters.
insights.surprise: The 2020 earthquake-safety bond (ESER) is also slow at 18%, while the 2019 affordable housing bond, often described as slow, had spent 72%.

insights.title: Residents grading city services A or B fell from 59% to 36% in eight years
insights.dek: The Controller's biennial City Survey shows the share of A or B grades for overall services peaking in 2015 and falling in every survey since, with the steepest drop between 2019 and 2021.
insights.why_it_matters: This is the only citywide outcome measure that asks residents directly, and it moved the opposite way from spending. Whether that is service quality, expectations or survey mode is exactly what the numbers cannot settle alone.
insights.surprise: The drop began in 2017, before the pandemic and before the FY2021 spending plateau.

insights.title: The median response to a life-threatening medical call is 63 seconds slower than in FY2013
insights.dek: Call-to-arrival went from 5 min 14 s to 6 min 17 s; dispatch-to-arrival from 3 min 27 s to 4 min 10 s. Both halves of the response got slower.
insights.why_it_matters: Survival for cardiac arrest falls with every minute before care arrives. A minute across 180,000 calls is a large change in outcomes that shows up in no budget document.

insights.title: Aid and grants account for a quarter of the $1.9B real growth in General Fund spending
insights.dek: Of the real increase between FY2013 and FY2025, salaries added $620M, fringe benefits $480M and aid and grants (mostly to nonprofits and individuals) $460M. Capital and other spending fell slightly.
insights.why_it_matters: The city's growth is not mainly a bigger workforce: aid and grants and fringe benefits together grew faster than salaries. That points to contracting and pension and health costs as the places to look.
insights.surprise: Overtime, the most discussed line, added $100M, about 5% of the growth.

insights.title: Departments whose spending grew most did not report better results than those held flat
insights.dek: Across 20 departments with at least four comparable measures, the correlation between real spending growth and the share of a department's own measures that improved is close to zero (r = 0.04).
insights.why_it_matters: This is the question the whole dashboard exists to ask. The honest answer from self-reported measures is that spending and reported performance are unrelated at the department level; that is either a finding about the city or a finding about the measures.
insights.surprise: Several departments with flat real spending, including City Administrator and the Airport, improved most of their measures.

insights.title: Three uniformed departments account for 84% of city overtime
insights.dek: Police, Fire and Sheriff paid $471M of the city's $560M overtime in FY2025. Overtime was 15–18% of pay in those departments and under 5% almost everywhere else.
insights.why_it_matters: Overtime debates are really debates about three departments' staffing models. The rest of the city runs on overtime at a level most employers would consider normal.

insights.title: A measure that missed its target was 44% more likely to be redefined the next year
insights.dek: After a miss, 4.2% of measures were redefined in the following report against 2.9% after a hit. Dropping a measure outright was only slightly more common after a miss (8.1% vs 7.3%).
insights.why_it_matters: Redefinition breaks the time series exactly where it was telling an uncomfortable story. Even when each change is justified, the pattern makes the measure set as a whole less informative than its size suggests.
insights.surprise: Dropping measures is not the mechanism; measures are dropped at nearly the same rate whether met or missed.

insights.title: Aid and grants rose from 16% to 24% of General Fund spending; salaries fell from 38% to 33%
insights.dek: The mix of what the General Fund buys has shifted steadily towards money paid out to nonprofits, individuals and other agencies, and away from the city's own payroll.
insights.why_it_matters: A city that delivers more through contracts needs different oversight than one that delivers through employees: contract monitoring, nonprofit financial health and grant outcomes rather than headcount and overtime.
insights.surprise: Fringe benefits, often described as the fastest-growing cost, held a steady 17–18% share.

insights.title: The June purchasing spike halved from 20% to 9%, then rebounded in FY2026
insights.dek: The share of purchase orders committed in the last month of the fiscal year fell every year from FY2018 to FY2025. In FY2026 it rose to 13%.
insights.why_it_matters: A June rush is the classic sign of use-it-or-lose-it budgeting. The decline suggests procurement reform worked; the rebound coincides with the FY2026 hiring freeze and deserves a look before it becomes a trend.
insights.surprise: The July share rose as the June share fell, so some of the improvement is a shift across the year boundary rather than smoother buying.

insights.title: Most departments spend within 5% of budget; City Administrator typically left 9% unspent
insights.dek: Over 14 years the median department spent 97% of what was appropriated. The City Attorney overspent by 6% in a typical year (billed back to client departments); City Administrator underspent by 9%, $247M cumulatively.
insights.why_it_matters: Persistent under-execution means money appropriated for services was not spent on them, and persistent over-execution means the adopted budget understates a department's real cost. Both weaken the budget as a public statement of intent.

insights.title: Real cost per library visit is up 67% since FY2017, while cost per fire incident fell 7%
insights.dek: Of nine curated cost-per-unit pairs, six rose faster than inflation. Library visits have not recovered to pre-pandemic levels while spending has; fire incident costs fell because incidents grew faster than the budget.
insights.why_it_matters: Unit costs are the closest the data gets to productivity. Where visits, cases or riders fall while spending holds, the city is paying more for each unit of service it delivers, whatever the reason.
insights.surprise: The Library's own reported cost per visit is lower ($20 nominal in FY2017) because it uses a narrower spending base; the direction is the same.

insights.title: Public Health commits 2.3 times a typical month's purchase orders in June
insights.dek: In a median year, DPH entered 15% of its annual purchase orders in the last month, about $150M. City Administrator (1.5×) and Homelessness (1.4×) also show a June spike; most other departments do not.
insights.why_it_matters: A department-level June rush pinpoints where a year-end habit lives. At DPH's scale, purchases pulled forward into June to protect an appropriation are large enough to matter for what the following year's budget looks like.
insights.surprise: Community Investment & Infrastructure commits almost nothing in June (0.05×), because its budget follows the calendar of bond and tax-increment funding rather than the fiscal year.

insights.title: Outcome measures are met less often than output measures: 58% vs 71%
insights.dek: In FY2025 departments met 71% of measures that count activity (visits, inspections, cases closed) but 58% of measures that describe a result (response times, condition scores, satisfaction).
insights.why_it_matters: A city can hit every activity target and still not deliver the result residents want. If the dashboard's 'share met' headline is mostly outputs, it flatters performance; reading outcomes separately is the fairer test.

insights.title: Per-resident human welfare spending grew 84%, three times the pace of public protection
insights.dek: Real spending per resident in the Human Welfare and Neighborhood Development group rose from $1,420 to $2,610 between FY2013 and FY2025. Public Protection rose 25%, and Culture and Recreation 23%.
insights.why_it_matters: The city's priorities are visible in where growth went. This is the clearest statement of them in the data, and it should be read alongside the outcome findings above for the same groups.
insights.surprise: Public Works, Transportation and Commerce is the largest group per resident because the Airport and SFPUC are in it, funded by fees rather than taxes.
